name: Digital Twins for Experiments
title: Digital Twins for Experiments
answer: Digital twins for experiments are computational replicas of a physical experimental setup, an instrument, a sample, or a full laboratory workflow, kept in sync with data from the real system. They cover everything from a single bioreactor or spectrometer to a multi-step protocol run by robots, and they are used to design experiments, predict outcomes, and test control strategies before touching physical materials. The scope includes the model of the apparatus, the experimental conditions, the measurement chain, and the data that flows between them. In laboratory automation and simulation, a twin is not just an offline simulation, because it is connected to the live experiment and updates as conditions change. This makes it useful for virtual commissioning, operator training, and continuous monitoring, not only for one-off predictions.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A digital twin for experiments runs on a mix of edge devices near the instruments, lab workstations, on-premises servers, and cloud resources, depending on latency and data volume. It needs reliable data acquisition from sensors and instruments, a message layer or historian to move and store time-series data, and a simulation engine that can execute physics-based or data-driven models. Common building blocks include Python-based modeling libraries, containerized services, and databases for experiment metadata and model versions. The site's catalogue lists 800 scientific models and 732 AI tools, which reflects the range of components that teams may draw on when assembling a twin. Security and network isolation matter because a twin often has write access to lab equipment or can influence experimental parameters.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts by defining the experimental asset and the protocol, then instrumenting the physical system so that the twin receives the same inputs and conditions as the real experiment. Teams build a model, often a hybrid of first-principles equations and machine learning, and calibrate it against historical runs or dedicated calibration experiments. Validation uses held-out experiments to check that the twin predicts measurable outcomes within an acceptable tolerance, and uncertainty is quantified so that predictions come with error bars. Once validated, the twin can run design of experiments, optimization, or reinforcement learning to propose new conditions, which are then tested in the physical lab and fed back to update the model. Version control, experiment tracking, and reproducible pipelines are part of the method, because a twin that cannot be traced back to its data and code is hard to trust.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk around digital twins for experiments include ownership of the data generated by the lab, licensing of simulation models and software, and intellectual property in the twin itself. Provenance requires recording where each data point came from, how it was transformed, which model version was used, and what calibration or validation steps were performed. Risk management covers model drift, silent failures, cyber security of connected instruments, and the possibility that a twin's prediction leads to wasted materials or unsafe conditions. When experiments involve human samples, animals, hazardous chemicals, or controlled agents, the twin must respect the same institutional reviews, safety rules, and export controls as the physical work. Practitioners typically keep audit trails and access controls so that a twin's recommendations can be reviewed before they affect a real experiment.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward closed-loop, self-driving laboratories where a digital twin continuously proposes experiments, a robot executes them, and the results update the twin without human intervention. Expect more integration with laboratory automation standards, better support for federated learning across institutions, and foundation models that can bootstrap a twin from limited data. The site's library currently holds 135 research papers and 12233 claims extracted from research works, which shows that the area is active and that claims are being catalogued for comparison. Over time, digital twins may become a standard part of experimental provenance, linking every result to a simulated counterpart and a versioned model. The main open questions are how to validate twins for regulated work, how to share them without losing control of sensitive data, and how to keep them aligned with physical systems that change over time.
